Trying to determine how much it could cost me to benchmark Muse Wonder...every other model I have benchmarked has been able to do it no problem, in a sub.

Muse Code's $50/mo tier and can't get through even all the tasks in my benchmark suite at low effort.

Looks like I would need a budget between $310-$770 to benchmark Muse Wonder vs. $0 for models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI since I can run those in my subs.

So...trying to think of alternate paths. I've been told that potentially Muse Code just might not be a super optimal harness, and Pi might be a better harness to use it with.

Might try this before calling it. Such a bummer because I really like the team at Meta, but I have no horse in this race and have to be independent and just let the data guide me.

And right now, I can't possibly understand why I would code with a model that is so much more expensive than the latest models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

But, not giving up yet, just can't put $500+ into benchmarking this if I already know I wouldn't recommend it for coding with the early cost-per-task data I'm seeing.

Next I'm going to compare a few tasks at low effort in Pi to see if the cost-per-task is lower than in Pi...hoping it's just the harness and not the model 🤞

There’s been a lot of discussion on Muse Wonder since the launch. But there are some very interesting aspects that are under-discussed and make this launch unique from the rest of the frontier:

1. Big model smell reporting (goodbye benchmaxxing?): For the first time, a model launch measured and reported big model smell which basically shows how the model does on tasks it targeted in post-training vs tasks it didn’t. 
It’s essentially a guard against “benchmaxxed” models. I haven’t seen another frontier lab put this in a launch post, and I think all labs should start reporting it, ideally with the held-out tasks named.

2. Active focus: Muse Wonder is built to not give up when it hits real-world blockers, to keep trying alternative approaches and adapt to new information, while checking in before important actions. For instance, if a dinner reservation fails or a form throws an error, it tries another route on its own. Every lab trains for persistence, but Meta measures it on everyday personal tasks like housing, travel, IT and finance, not just coding. That’s what makes Wonder a good fit for assistants like Muse.

Active memory: carries important context about you across conversations and pulls up the details that matter for whatever you’re doing. This release tested it inside long chats where facts change. 
Early in a long chat you say “my flight is tuesday”, then 50K tokens of other stuff later you say “actually it moved to thursday”. Ask “when do I fly?” and a model with weak memory might say tuesday because it saw that first. Meta built their memory test around exactly this case (and wonder tops it). Imo this stale info problem is the hardest part of memory, way harder than just remembering stuff. 

Memory+focus are so important for assistants. Muse will eat the world. 

public source in comment below.

Very early impressions of Muse Wonder in the Muse app:

1. No regressions I notice. In particular, no personality or writing regressions. Feels like the same entity I was talking to with Spark.

2. Better UI sense. Had it polish an app made with Spark and it found a really elegant way of positioning a footer “Next” button that kept going off screen in a quiz (it floated the button so it always stays in the same place rather than getting pushed down).

3. Caught subtle bugs in that same app. Not major ones, but ones that required a close reading of the code and understanding of how it was supposed to work and actually worked.

One thing that’s not clear right now is whether Wonder also powers background tasks like goal summaries and the news feed. My current feeling is yes to to the news feed and no to the goal summaries based on how they’re still written (have some of the really bad AI writing tells, like trying too hard to have a voice, and self-referentially calling attention to things that they only need to show rather than also tell).
